The one-step distillation addresses a real computational bottleneck and makes the diffusion-derived signal much more practically usable.
The paper is generally well organized and includes useful limitations on satellite and medical domains rather than presenting the method as universally reliable.
weaknesses: Some headline claims are overstated. Comparisons to point-supervised or open-vocabulary methods are not fully apples-to-apples because TRACE relies on very large pretrained diffusion models, large-scale image-text pretraining, and nontrivial compute.

Reproducibility is not yet fully convincing: exact attention layers/hooks, preprocessing, thresholding details, LoRA/fine-tuning schedules, checkpoint availability, and BGP implementation choices need to be specified more concretely.

The instance-edge benchmark based on COCO panoptic boundaries reports extremely high ODS/OIS values; this needs more careful protocol detail, including boundary thickness/tolerance, threshold selection, and whether any validation/test leakage is possible.

The theoretical explanation of IEP relies on idealized assumptions such as time-invariant clean similarities and scalar inverse temperature dynamics; it is useful intuition but should not be presented as strong theoretical justification for real diffusion transformers.
The absolute UIS AP values remain low despite large relative gains, so the practical significance for standalone instance segmentation should be framed more cautiously.
There are a few clarity and consistency issues, such as differing reported gains, minor typos, and occasional ambiguity about when TRACE is training-free versus fine-tuned.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and potentially useful phenomenon: diffusion self-attention appears to contain transient instance-boundary information that can be exploited without mask, box, or point annotations.
The proposed pipeline is conceptually simple, with clear components for timestep selection, attention-boundary scoring, one-step distillation, and downstream mask refinement.
The manuscript includes many experiments, ablations, backbone comparisons, and some failure-case analysis, which is more thorough than many weakly supervised segmentation submissions.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially over-stated. The evidence supports diffusion features as a useful boundary prior, but not the much stronger claim that diffusion models are secretly instance edge detectors or a scalable replacement for annotation.

The evaluation raises fairness concerns. TRACE uses very large text-to-image diffusion backbones and costly pretraining/fine-tuning, while several comparisons are against smaller or older baselines; the paper repeatedly frames this as annotation-free without adequately accounting for the supervision and data baked into the diffusion models.
Absolute performance in unsupervised instance segmentation remains very low on COCO/VOC despite relative gains, so the practical significance is weaker than the framing suggests.

The weakly supervised panoptic comparisons are not fully convincing: gains depend on coupling TRACE with strong semantic models and sometimes larger backbones, making it hard to isolate whether TRACE itself fairly surpasses point-supervised methods.

The instance-edge benchmark and very high ODS/OIS numbers are under-specified and potentially inflated. Details such as boundary thickness, matching tolerance, train/evaluation separation, and whether the benchmark favors TRACE-style outputs are not sufficiently clear.

The theoretical analysis relies on highly simplified assumptions, such as time-invariant clean similarities and a scalar inverse-temperature schedule, that do not describe real diffusion transformer attention. It is therefore more intuition than technical justification.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a method with many moving parts: exact attention layers, training data, loss weights, LoRA placement, BGP parameters, decoder architecture, and evaluation protocols are not specified at the level needed to reproduce the results reliably.

The paper has presentation issues and recurring overclaims, including calling some settings training-free despite relying on a separately trained/distilled TRACE module and underplaying the reported 8-10 day training cost and high VRAM requirements.

strengths: The core idea is interesting: using diffusion-model self-attention as an instance-boundary prior is a plausible and potentially useful direction for unsupervised or weakly supervised segmentation.

The paper makes a serious effort to evaluate across several downstream settings, including UIS, weakly supervised panoptic segmentation, open-vocabulary segmentation, ablations, runtime, and failure cases.
The proposed pipeline is modular and practically motivated: IEP/ABDiv provide pseudo edges, and distillation attempts to make inference much cheaper than per-image diffusion analysis.
weaknesses: The main claims are substantially overstated. Phrases such as annotation-free, training-free, and diffusion models secretly being instance edge detectors are not well supported, since the method relies on large pretrained diffusion models, LoRA fine-tuning, an edge decoder, pseudo-label training, downstream segmentation systems, and sometimes large semantic backbones.

The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently clear or fair. It is ambiguous whether TRACE is trained on ImageNet, target training images, or evaluation images in different tables; calling some settings training-free while reporting 8-10 days of training is misleading. These ambiguities make the reported gains difficult to interpret.

Comparisons to point-supervised and open-vocabulary methods are not fully controlled. TRACE often benefits from very large external generative priors and stronger backbones, while the baselines are not given comparable priors or refinement machinery, weakening the claim that tags plus TRACE genuinely surpass point supervision.

The edge-quality results are suspiciously strong and insufficiently justified. An ODS of 0.889 against COCO instance boundaries from an annotation-free pipeline is extraordinary, but the paper does not rule out transductive fitting, evaluation leakage, metric artifacts, boundary thickness effects, or thresholding choices.

Several technical details needed for reproducibility are missing or vague: exact attention layers, spatial alignment of HW-by-HW attention maps across resolutions, edge decoder architecture, training schedule, learning rates, BGP hyperparameters, random-walk parameters, and dataset-specific choices.

The information-theoretic analysis is weak. It assumes a highly simplified attention model with time-invariant logits and a scalar inverse-temperature schedule, which does not match real diffusion transformers; the resulting Fisher-information argument does not establish that the selected timestep corresponds to instance emergence.

Ablations do not isolate the contribution cleanly. The large jump from raw IEP+ABDiv to distilled TRACE suggests that the learned decoder and fine-tuning may be doing much of the work, but there is no strong control against simpler pseudo-edge training, supervised boundary detectors adapted to the same data, SAM automatic masks, or diffusion-feature baselines under the same refinement pipeline.

The absolute UIS performance remains very low on challenging datasets despite relative gains, and the paper’s language often presents these results as much more practically decisive than the numbers justify.

Limitations on tiny objects and medical imagery are reported, which is good, but they also reveal that the method is strongly tied to natural-image diffusion priors and may fail in important domains where instance segmentation is valuable.

Ablations are unusually thorough: the paper isolates IEP, ABDiv, distillation, similarity metrics, prompt usage, decoder capacity, edge alternatives, and multiple diffusion/non-diffusion backbones.
The one-step distillation makes the approach much more practical, reducing expensive per-image diffusion analysis while preserving or improving boundary quality.
The paper is generally clear, well positioned, and includes useful limitations on satellite and medical imagery rather than hiding failure modes.
weaknesses: The annotation-free/training-free framing is somewhat overstated: TRACE relies on large pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, ImageNet self-distillation, and substantial training cost, so comparisons to truly training-free UIS pipelines are not perfectly aligned.

Reproducibility details are still incomplete despite the appendix: exact training schedule, learning rates/batch sizes/epochs, edge decoder architecture, BGP hyperparameters, preprocessing, and checkpoint/code availability need to be specified more concretely.

Some comparisons need more qualification. The weakly supervised panoptic gains partly involve stronger backbones and very large generative priors, while the open-vocabulary/SAM comparisons are under-specified and may not be fully apples-to-apples.

The reported instance-edge quality is strikingly high relative to downstream AP, and the boundary benchmark construction/evaluation tolerance should be clarified and compared against stronger supervised or instance-boundary-specific baselines.
The method has clear limitations for tiny objects and out-of-distribution imagery, and the paper does not deeply discuss inherited biases or failure modes from the pretrained diffusion backbones.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: the paper identifies a useful instance-boundary signal in diffusion self-attention and operationalizes it through IEP, ABDiv, and one-step edge distillation.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall, covering unsupervised instance segmentation, tag-supervised panoptic segmentation, edge-quality evaluation, open-vocabulary extensions, multiple datasets, and multiple diffusion/non-diffusion backbones.

Ablations are unusually comprehensive: component ablations, similarity metrics, decoder capacity, prompt sensitivity, backbone comparisons, and explicit failure cases all support the main design choices.
The method is practically attractive as a plug-in boundary prior for existing segmentation pipelines, and the distillation step addresses the otherwise prohibitive per-image diffusion probing cost.
The paper is candid about important limitations on tiny satellite objects and out-of-distribution medical imagery, which improves the credibility of the evaluation.
weaknesses: Some claims are overstated. The framing that diffusion models are inherently instance edge detectors is stronger than what is shown; the final system also depends on thresholding, pseudo-label distillation, LoRA fine-tuning, and downstream propagation.

Fairness of comparison should be qualified more carefully: TRACE relies on very large web-scale diffusion backbones and substantial compute, while several baselines are much smaller or use different pretrained resources.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a top-tier submission: learning rates, batch sizes, number of epochs, LoRA target modules, decoder architecture details, random seeds/variance, and code or checkpoint release plans are not sufficiently specified.
The unsupervised instance segmentation AP values remain low in absolute terms despite large relative gains, so the practical significance of the UIS results should be framed more cautiously.

Several auxiliary comparisons, especially TRACE+SAM/open-vocabulary detector results, are less rigorously tabulated than the main experiments, and some numerical/textual inconsistencies remain, such as the satellite AP drop reported in Table 14.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and potentially useful signal: diffusion self-attention appears to contain transient instance-boundary information, and the IEP/ABDiv formulation is a plausible way to expose it.

The method is evaluated across several downstream settings, including unsupervised instance segmentation, weakly supervised panoptic segmentation, edge quality, multiple diffusion backbones, and some out-of-domain failure cases.
The reported gains over MaskCut/ProMerge-style UIS baselines are large, and the ablations suggest that timestep selection, divergence-based boundary scoring, and distillation each contribute.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims feel overextended relative to the evidence. The instance-edge benchmark reports extremely high ODS/OIS scores, but the construction, tolerance, train/test separation, thresholding, and possible evaluation artifacts are not described sufficiently to make the result convincing.

Comparisons are not always fair or cleanly interpreted. TRACE is presented as annotation-free or training-free in places, yet it requires diffusion fine-tuning/distillation, substantial ImageNet training, and downstream Mask2Former training for panoptic results. This makes the comparison to truly training-free UIS and point-supervised methods hard to interpret.

Reproducibility is weak for a method with many moving parts. Key details such as learning rate, training duration/epochs, batch size, exact training data, LoRA target modules, attention layers used, edge decoder architecture, BGP/random-walk hyperparameters, and post-processing are missing or only vaguely inherited from baselines.

Several claims are misleading or insufficiently supported, including 'secretly an instance edge detector,' 'real-time' inference for an 8B diffusion backbone, and surpassing point-supervised panoptic methods when the strongest comparisons are small and sometimes involve different backbones.

The theoretical appendix is not persuasive: it assumes attention rows follow a simple time-varying-temperature exponential family with fixed clean similarities, which does not reflect the actual changing hidden states and Q/K projections in diffusion transformers. It does not establish that KL peaks correspond to instance boundaries.

There are numerical and presentation errors that undermine confidence, e.g. Table 14 reports 65.4 to 50.3 as a -5.1 drop instead of -15.1, and some runtime/overhead statements conflict with the reported 8-10 day training and 20-32GB VRAM requirements.

Important baselines are discussed but not quantitatively compared in the main downstream evaluations, especially diffusion-based segmentation methods such as DiffCut/DiffSeg/EmerDiff-style approaches and stronger open-vocabulary or SAM-based pipelines under matched supervision and compute.

Overall, the idea is interesting, but the paper currently has enough issues in evaluation validity, clarity of supervision/compute, reproducibility, and claim calibration that I would not consider it competitive for acceptance at a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: Interesting central observation that diffusion self-attention may contain transient instance-boundary cues, and the IEP/ABDiv formulation is simple and potentially useful.
The paper attempts broad empirical coverage across unsupervised instance segmentation, weakly supervised panoptic segmentation, edge quality, several diffusion backbones, and additional domains.
Component ablations for IEP, ABDiv, distillation, KL vs. alternatives, decoder capacity, and uncertainty masking help clarify what parts of the pipeline matter.
The authors include some negative results on satellite and medical imagery, which is a useful limitation disclosure.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated. TRACE is presented as annotation-free/training-free and low-overhead, but the method uses large diffusion backbones, an 8-10 day ImageNet distillation stage, image tags for panoptic segmentation, and downstream model training in several settings.

The comparisons are not fully convincing. TRACE adds a very large diffusion model and learned edge decoder to much lighter UIS baselines, while the weakly supervised panoptic claims depend on changing supervision, backbone strength, and downstream training protocols.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the claimed scale: key details such as learning rate, epochs, batch size, exact distillation data, selected attention layers, seed/noise handling, postprocessing thresholds, and split definitions are missing or only deferred to prior work.

Several numbers and claims appear internally inconsistent or suspicious: runtime overhead is described as 2%, 6%, and 81x faster in different places; Table 14 has an arithmetic error; and the reported 0.889 ODS for unsupervised instance-edge detection on COCO panoptic boundaries is extraordinary without enough validation.

The technical justification is weak. IEP and ABDiv are KL-based heuristics, and the information-theoretic derivation relies on unrealistic assumptions about time-invariant logits and a scalar inverse temperature; it does not establish that the KL peak corresponds to true instance boundaries.

The evaluation lacks stronger controls: no statistical variation, limited fairness analysis for reproduced baselines, insufficient comparison to learned boundary/segmentation alternatives trained under comparable compute, and unclear tuning of conventional edge detector baselines in the BGP pipeline.

Novelty is moderate rather than decisive: using diffusion attention for segmentation is already an active line of work, and the paper’s contribution is mainly a combination of timestep selection, local attention divergence, pseudo-label distillation, and known propagation machinery.
Absolute UIS performance remains low despite relative gains, so the practical significance is less compelling than the framing suggests.
